newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugo dinar to devalue on political decision only.
newsitem.headline: Yugo dinar to devalue on political decision only.

text.p: The Yugoslav financial market has cautiously expressed its fear of a possible dinar devaluation after the Sunday elections, but economists said on Thursday any decision to devalue would be purely political.
Traders on the Belgrade bourse said market activity was subdued ahead of the Sunday federal and local elections in Yugoslavia and fears of a devaluation soon after the polls.

"With 1993 mega-inflation (when it ran at 60 percent a day) in mind, there is still a fear of the history repeating itself," Biljana Stojanovic of the Belgrade-based Institute of Economic Sciences told Reuters.
Yugoslav exports are weak, industrial output growth low and still not back to its realistic levels, she said.
"But officials are aware of those fears and will not abandon the fixed dinar rate. It is a psychological factor."
Without a genuine foreign exchange market, the level of the dinar exchange rate would be determined purely on arbitrary basis, she said.
The National Bank of Yugoslavia (NBY) and the government have repeated their firm commitment to a stable dinar in 1997.

"NBY has a tiny space to play with the dinar rate. We shall retain the fixed rate and the currency board mechanism (of base money creation)," a senior NBY official who asked not to be named told Reuters.
Even a slight effort to relax the currency board mechanism proved to be dangerous for the Yugoslav monetary stability.

"Earlier attempts to diverge from the currency board mechanism (such as end-1994) provoked inflation and a surge in the black market exchange rate," CES-Mecon, private institute for economic research, said in its October country report prepared for the United Nations Economic Commission For Europe.

A government economist said Yugoslavia had a bad experience with floating in the past. "We may have a less rigid fixed rate but money from the International Monetary Fund would be used to create the dinar stabilisation fund," Oskar Kovac said.
The central bank intervention on the interbank forex market is the key to dinar stability, Biljana Stojanovic said, adding a devaluation would be a matter of a political will.

It is clear that prices began to rise faster after the current dinar rate was set in November 1995. "The dinar was devalued by 70 percent to reach 3.3 per to a German mark," said Bosko Zivkovic of the CES-Mecon.
Zivkovic said the key to the current 11-month currency stability were low wages and a slightly improved access to foreign currency after the sanctions were lifted.

"With low wages, Yugoslavs are forced to sell their hard currency savings," he said and added that a possible destabilisation could be expected if wages begin to rise in real terms. The average wage stands at 200 German marks.
Exporters could benefit from a devalued dinar, but economists saw no reason to meet their expectations yet.

Danko Djunic, head of the Economics Institute said it was wrong for the exporters to seek a solution in saying the dinar rate was inadequate. "A dinar devaluation would not solve problems while there are no attempts to restructure," he said. -- Gordana Filipovic, Belgrade newsroom, +381 11 222 4254
